nāda
(‘vibration,’ ‘sound’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word ‘nāda’ is generally used in the sense of sound—both unmanifest and manifest—it has been employed more as a technical term in शैविस्म् and the शाक्त-तन्त्रस्.
Before च्रेअतिओन्, the शिव-शक्ति principle—the ultimate Reality—is one only, without a second. When this Reality—the equivalent of ब्रह्मन् of the Advaita Vedānta—starts reflecting on Itself (which is called ‘vimarṣa’) a throb or a stir is created. This stir named as स्पन्द, develops further as ‘nāda’ or vibration, and gets concentrated as ‘bindu’ (point of tremendous energy). Further च्रेअतिओन् evolves out of it.
When the word is taken to mean sound, several varieties of it are described in the technical works related to मुसिच् and yogic practices. For instance: ghaṇṭānāda (sound of a bell); śaṅkhanāda (sound of a conch); bherīnāda (sound of a kettle-drum); veṇunāda (sound of a flute); मेघनाद (sound of clouds or thunder) and so on.

Nadīstuti
(‘hymn in praise of the rivers [like Sindhū and सरस्वती]’)
------------------------------------------
This सूक्त or hymn in praise of the well-known rivers of that time appears in the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā (10.7

). There are nine ṛks or mantras.
The first मन्त्र is in praise of all the waters of all the seven rivers.
The next three mantras are addressed to the river Sindhū along with its tribu-taries. These tributaries approach the Sindhū like little children their मोथेर्, or, the calves the मोथेर्-cow.
The fifth मन्त्र is very important since it names ten prominent rivers of those times, from गङ्गा, यमुना and सरस्वती up to Suṣomā (See NADĪ also.).
The rest of the mantras again—four in number—are in praise of Sindhū, not only as a nourishing river, but also as a goddess.

Nādabindūpaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad in 53 verses and has been assigned to the Ṛgveda.
It starts with a description of the प्रणव or ओङ्कार as a bird with the four syllables (a, u, m and the ardhamātrā, the unmanifest last half-syllable) forming the various parts of its body. Similarly the three guṇas, धर्म (righteousness) and अधर्म (unrighteousness), the seven lokas or worlds (from bhūḥ or earth up to ब्रह्मलोक or the world of ब्रह्मा) are also described as the various parts of this bird.
An adept in योग who rides this हṁस or swan, will not be affected by the kārmic effects of even millions of births.
Then comes a description of meditation on the four syllables of the प्रणव or ओङ्कार. They should be considered as related to the deities अग्नि (fire-god), वायु (wind-god), Bhānu (sun-god) and वरुण (god of the oceans and water).
Each of the four mātras can be subdivided into three parts (either depending on time as past, present and future, or the mode of uttering it as उदात्त [medium tone or scale], अनुदात्त [one scale below] and स्वरित [one scale above]). This makes the total twelve. Each of these is given a particular name like ghoṣiṇī, vidyunmātra, pataṅginī and so on.
The next group of verses gives the result of leaving the body at the time of uttering any one of these twelve aspects of प्रणव. For instance, one who dies while contemplating upon the first mātrā is born again as an emperor. If it is on the fourth, he will attain the world of the गन्धर्वस्. If on the ninth, he will be reborn in the महर्लोक, and so on.
Then, the Upaniṣad describes the result of getting the मिन्द् dissolved in the Supreme शिव. He is rid of all bondages and attains the ever-blissful ब्रह्मन्.
After this the Upaniṣad discusses whether the jñāni (the realised सोउल्) has प्रारब्धकर्म (the कर्म responsible for this birth) or not. The conclusion is that though it is there, he does not feel it, since the whole life is like a dream to him.
Now comes a description of the योगि sitting in the siddhāsana (a posture specially recommended for meditation) with vaiṣṇavīmudrā (keeping the eyelids without blinking, the eyes apparently seeing outside, but the मिन्द् withdrawn inside). The योगि is then able to hear the internal sound through the right ear. He should concentrate on this so that he becomes deaf as it were, to all external sounds.
In this sādhanā or practice, he will hear many types of sound similar to those of ocean waves, kettle-drums, bell and horn. Then he may hear the sounds similar to the tinkling of bells, flute, humming of bees and so on. However, he should shift his concentration from gross sounds to subtler sounds. Merging of the मिन्द् totally in such sounds gives him the realisation of चिदाकाश or the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् in the space of the heart.
The प्रणव (Oṅkāra) is ब्रह्मन् which, again, is full of effulgence (of pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्). When the मिन्द् is dissolved in this, the योगि is fully liberated and is—as if—dead to the phenomenal world.
The Upaniṣad ends with a short description of the mukta-पुरुष (liberated सोउल्) which is similar to such descriptions given in the Bhagavadgītā.

nādānusandhāna
(‘meditation on the sound’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the methods described by the works on हठयोग for the लय or dissolution of the मिन्द्.
Sitting in the muktāsana (a posture similar to siddhāsana, good for meditation) and practising the शाम्भवीमुद्रा (intent gazing at a minute object until tears flow) the योगि should hear the नाद or sound produced by सṁयम (perfect concentration) (vide Yogasūtras 3.4) on the सुषुम्ना.
This नादानुसन्धान has four stages all of which have to be learnt from competent teachers of हठयोग.
It leads to complete control over the मिन्द् and the senses.

nadī
(‘[water that flows] by making sound,’ ‘river’)
------------------------------------------
Rivers have always been looked upon, in the Hindu scriptures, with awe and reverence. They have also been—at least the major ones—deified and accepted as goddesses. This may be because they are sources of life-giving water (not only for drinking but also for raising crops). Again, their banks provided the ṛṣis and munis (sages) with a congenial place for practising austerities. This might have led to the belief that bathing in them purifies not only the body but also the मिन्द्.
The Ṛgveda itself mentions 20 rivers by name (vide 5.53.9; 10.64.9; 10.75.5,6) and refers to another 99 flowing rivers later (10.104.8).
If a flowing water has to be called a ‘nadī’ or river it had to be at least of a length of 8000 धनुस् (14.4 kms.).
Only the nadīs that flowed directly into the sea were considered holy or pure enough for taking a bath.
In the Ṛgveda (10.75.5-6) there is a Nadīstuti, a eulogy of seven important rivers. They are: गङ्गा, यमुना, सरस्वती, शुतुद्री, Paruṣṇī, Marudvṛdhā and Ārjīkīyā.
In this verse itself, three more rivers are also mentioned: असिक्नी, वितस्ता and Suṣomā.
The rivers गङ्गा and यमुना are very much there even now and command great reverence from the Hindus.
Sarasvatī, once a mighty river, is believed to have disappeared underground, probably around 2000 B. C.
The other rivers have been identified by the scholars of Indology as follows:
ancient present
Ārjīkīyā Vipāśā
Asiknī Chenab
Marudvṛdhā Maruvārdvān
Paruṣṇī Rāvī
Suṣomā Sohān
Śutudrī Sutlej
Vitastā Jhelum

The Ṛgveda also mentions the Sapta-sindhūs (seven great rivers) vide 1.32.12; 1.34.8; 4.28.1; 10.43.3) which are the same as the Sindhū (Indus), सरस्वती and the five rivers of Punjab.
Even in the modern days, seven rivers are highly venerated and their presence invoked into the water used for पूजा or ritualistic worship. They are: गङ्गा, यमुना, गोदावरी, सरस्वती, नर्मदा, Sindhū and कावेरी.
Water is the greatest gift of God to living beings. Rivers and lakes are the lifeline of a nation. According to the पुराणस्, a sage Tundila by name, worshipped शिव, the great God, and became one of his aspects, viz., water. He came to be called पुष्कर or Water-god. When ब्रह्मा created this world he took the help of पुष्कर, as also बृहस्पति, the sage-preceptor of the gods. According to the arrangement arrived at among them, whenever बृहस्पति (represented by the planet गुरु or जुपितेर्) enters a particular zodiacal sign, a particular river becomes a ‘Puṣkara,’ charged with the divine power of all the gods. This happens once in 12 years for each of the twelve rivers mentioned in the पुराणस्. And, that power will last for 12 days. So, whosoever takes a dip in that river at its पुष्कर-period, is benefited immensely in the spiritual sense.
The following table serves as a guide for the puṣkaras of important rivers:
When बृहस्पति enters the zodiac Puṣkara commences for
1. Meṣa (Aries) Gaṅgā
2. Vṛṣabha (Taurus) Narmadā
3. Mithuna (Gemini) Sarasvatī
4. Karkāṭaka (Cancer) Yamunā
5. Siṁha (Leo) Godāvarī
6. कन्या (Virgo) Kṛṣṇā
7. Tulā (Libra) Kāverī
8. Vṛścika (Scorpio) Tāmraparṇī
9. धनुस् (Sagittarius) Sindhū
10. मकर (Capricorn) Tuṅgabhadrā
11. Kumbha (Aquarine) Bhīmarathī
12. Mīna (Pisces) Praṇahitā (Tapatī)

Naturally, during these periods of पुष्कर of a particular river, thousands of devout people gather there, to have a ceremonial dip in that river and earn religious merit.
